page.mentor_intro: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) is an ophthalmic emergency where neurosensory retina separates from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium due to a full-thickness retinal tear. Prompt diagnosis and emergency vitreo-retinal surgical intervention are essential to preserve visual acuity.

teaching_points.claim: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) is the most common form, developing when acute posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) produces vitreoretinal traction, causing a full-thickness retinal break that allows liquefied vitreous humor to enter the subretinal space.

Classic clinical presentation features sudden-onset photopsia (flashes of light caused by mechanical vitreoretinal traction), a sudden shower of floaters (often dark specks or 'cobwebs' representing microvascular hemorrhage), followed by a progressive, dark, non-painful visual field curtain or shadow advancing from the periphery.

Immediate funduscopic assessment must determine macular status: 'macula-on' retinal detachment (fovea remains attached with preserved central visual acuity) represents an absolute ocular emergency requiring surgical reattachment within 24 to 72 hours to prevent irreversible visual loss; 'macula-off' detachment carries worse visual prognosis and can be scheduled semi-electively within 7 to 10 days.

Primary surgical interventions include pars plana vitrectomy (PPV, excision of vitreous with internal gas or silicone oil tamponade and endolaser), pneumatic retinopexy (intravitreal gas bubble injection with outpatient positioning for superior single breaks), and scleral buckling (external silicon band indentation to relieve traction in young, phakic eyes).

Urgent management while awaiting emergency surgical transfer includes keeping the patient strictly fasting, maintaining positioning that keeps the retinal tear dependent to prevent gravitational progression toward the macula, and avoiding eye rubbing.

uncertainties: Efficacy of prophylactic laser retinopexy to asymptomatic peripheral lattice degeneration in fellow eyes of patients with giant retinal tears.
Long-term visual outcomes of pneumatic retinopexy versus primary pars plana vitrectomy for uncomplicated superior rhegmatogenous detachments (PIVOT trial data).
mcq_angles: Surgical urgency determination: 'macula-on' retinal detachment requires emergency repair within 24–72 hours to preserve central vision; 'macula-off' has lower surgical urgency.
Premonitory symptoms of retinal tear/detachment: photopsia (flashes) and a sudden shower of floaters, followed by a curtain-like peripheral visual field defect.
Surgical modality in young phakic patients: scleral buckling preserves the natural crystalline lens and avoids vitrectomy-induced nuclear sclerotic cataract progression.

page.mentor_intro: Retroperitoneal sarcomas (RPS) are rare mesodermal malignancies that typically present late as large, asymptomatic abdominal masses. Complete compartmental surgical resection with microscopically negative margins (R0/R1) by a specialized sarcoma multidisciplinary team represents the only curative modality, as local recurrence remains the predominant mode of failure.

teaching_points.claim: Retroperitoneal sarcomas (predominantly liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma) are characterized by insidious growth within the compliant retroperitoneal space; percutaneous core needle biopsy (retroperitoneal/flank approach avoiding transperitoneal seeding) is mandatory before any intervention to establish histological subtype and grade.

Complete macroscopically negative surgical resection (R0 or R1) performed en bloc with involved contiguous organs (e.g., kidney, colon, psoas fascia) in a high-volume specialized sarcoma center is the cornerstone of curative therapy and the strongest predictor of long-term disease-specific survival.

Well-differentiated liposarcomas (WDLPS) and dedifferentiated liposarcomas (DDLPS) are driven by MDM2 and CDK4 gene amplifications on chromosome 12q, which can be identified by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to differentiate them from benign lipomatous neoplasms.

The phase III STRASS trial demonstrated that routine preoperative radiotherapy did not significantly improve abdominal recurrence-free survival in unselected retroperitoneal sarcoma, though post-hoc subgroup analyses suggested potential locoregional benefit specifically in low-grade well-differentiated liposarcoma.

Leiomyosarcomas arise from retroperitoneal smooth muscle or major venous structures (inferior vena cava); IVC leiomyosarcomas require careful vascular planning for en bloc vascular resection and reconstruction (prosthetic PTFE graft or primary venorrhaphy).

uncertainties: Role of neoadjuvant histology-tailored chemotherapy (doxorubicin/ifosfamide) in high-grade dedifferentiated liposarcoma (STRASS 2 trial evaluation).
Therapeutic threshold for re-resection versus palliative systemic therapy in multifocal retroperitoneal recurrence.
mcq_angles: Preoperative biopsy route: retroperitoneal flank approach under CT/ultrasound guidance is essential to avoid contaminating the peritoneal cavity.
Diagnostic hallmark of liposarcoma: MDM2 gene amplification detected by FISH distinguishes well-differentiated liposarcoma from benign lipoma.
Primary mode of failure in retroperitoneal sarcoma: locoregional recurrence (accounting for ~75% of disease-specific deaths), contrasting with extremity sarcomas where distant metastases dominate.

page.mentor_intro: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin and muscle contents after muscle injury; the main danger is acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia. Early large-volume intravenous fluid is the mainstay.

teaching_points.claim: Causes include trauma and crush injury, exertion, seizures, immobilisation, drugs (statins, cocaine), toxins, infection and metabolic or genetic muscle disorders; creatine kinase above about 5 times the upper limit confirms it.

Early aggressive intravenous isotonic crystalloid is the main way to prevent myoglobin-induced acute tubular injury; fluid is titrated to a urine output of about 200 to 300 mL/hour and to avoid overload.
Routine sodium bicarbonate or mannitol is not recommended (EAST conditional recommendation); bicarbonate can worsen hypocalcaemia.

Treat hyperkalaemia, avoid calcium unless there is symptomatic hypocalcaemia or severe hyperkalaemia, and use renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, or volume overload; myoglobin is poorly cleared by standard dialysis.

In RhD-negative pregnant women, routine antenatal anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis is administered at 28 weeks of gestation and within 72 hours of potential fetomaternal hemorrhage events; when maternal anti-D alloimmunization is established, serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) Doppler ultrasonography non-invasively monitors for fetal anemia, guiding intrauterine red blood cell transfusion when velocities exceed 1.5 multiples of the median (MoM).

Intrauterine red blood cell transfusion via cordocentesis into the umbilical vein is the definitive treatment for severe fetal anemia, reversing hydrops fetalis with survival rates exceeding 90% in experienced fetal medicine centers.

page.mentor_intro: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains a leading cause of valvular morbidity worldwide, predominantly manifesting as rheumatic mitral stenosis (MS). Thromboembolism is a devastating complication, and anticoagulation principles differ fundamentally from non-valvular atrial fibrillation.

teaching_points.claim: Rheumatic mitral stenosis (moderate-to-severe, valve area <=1.5 cm2) is classified as 'valvular' heart disease; oral anticoagulation with Vitamin K Antagonists (warfarin, target INR 2.0 to 3.0) is the guideline-mandated standard of care for stroke prevention in the presence of atrial fibrillation, prior thromboembolism, or left atrial thrombus.

The landmark INVICTUS randomized controlled trial in rheumatic heart disease with atrial fibrillation established that warfarin was significantly superior to direct oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban), demonstrating lower rates of stroke and cardiovascular death without a significant difference in major bleeding.

Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs: dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) are contraindicated or not recommended in patients with moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis or mechanical prosthetic valves based on trial evidence (INVICTUS and RE-ALIGN).

Anticoagulation with warfarin is recommended even in sinus rhythm if rheumatic mitral stenosis is accompanied by a severely enlarged left atrium (left atrial diameter >50 mm or volume index >60 mL/m2), spontaneous echocardiographic contrast ('smoke'), or prior systemic embolism.

Secondary antibiotic prophylaxis against recurrent Group A streptococcal infection (intramuscular benzathine penicillin G every 3 to 4 weeks) is mandatory alongside anticoagulation to prevent progressive valvular scarring and deterioration.

uncertainties: Safety and efficacy of factor XI inhibitors in preventing left atrial thrombosis in rheumatic mitral stenosis.
Target INR optimization (2.0-3.0 vs 2.5-3.5) in patients with rheumatic mitral stenosis and spontaneous echocardiographic dense left atrial contrast.
mcq_angles: INVICTUS trial evidence: warfarin is superior to DOACs (rivaroxaban) for stroke prevention and all-cause mortality in rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF.
Definition of 'valvular AF': atrial fibrillation occurring in the presence of moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve.
Anticoagulation in sinus rhythm: indicated in rheumatic MS with left atrial thrombus, prior thromboembolism, or spontaneous echo contrast.

page.mentor_intro: The 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis prioritize early disease recognition to enable prompt disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) initiation before irreversible erosive joint damage occurs. Classification combines joint distribution, serology, acute-phase reactants, and symptom duration.

teaching_points.claim: The 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria utilize a score-based algorithm across four domains: joint involvement (0-5 points), serology with RF or anti-CCP (0-3 points), acute-phase reactants CRP/ESR (0-1 point), and symptom duration >=6 weeks (0-1 point), with a cumulative score of >=6/10 defining definite rheumatoid arthritis.

Anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (anti-CCP / ACPA) demonstrate high diagnostic specificity (>95%) for rheumatoid arthritis and independently predict aggressive radiographic erosive progression, often preceding clinical arthritis by several years.

Rheumatoid factor (RF) has moderate sensitivity (60-80%) but lower specificity (approx. 80-85%), occurring in primary Sjogren syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, chronic hepatitis C, subacute bacterial endocarditis, and healthy elderly individuals.

Symmetric polyarthritis classically involves the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and wrist joints, while characteristically sparing the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, thoracolumbar spine, and sacroiliac joints.

uncertainties: Classification accuracy of 2010 criteria in early seronegative elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritis.
Prognostic significance of dual-seropositive (RF+ and ACPA+) versus isolated ACPA seropositivity in predicting biologic response.
mcq_angles: Joint distribution scoring under 2010 criteria: involvement of >10 joints with at least 1 small joint yields maximum 5 points.
Differentiating RA from nodal osteoarthritis: sparing of DIP joints and presence of prolonged morning stiffness (>30-60 minutes).
Serological interpretation: high-titer ACPA (>3 times upper limit of normal) yields 3 points and dictates early aggressive DMARD combination.

page.mentor_intro: Biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs and tsDMARDs) have revolutionized rheumatoid arthritis care. Following inadequate response to conventional synthetic DMARDs, treatment escalates to TNF inhibitors, IL-6 receptor antagonists, T-cell costimulation modulators, B-cell depleters, or Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors.

teaching_points.claim: Biologic DMARDs are indicated in active RA with inadequate response or intolerance to conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate); combination of a biologic (e.g., TNF inhibitor or IL-6 inhibitor) with methotrexate is significantly more effective at achieving clinical remission and preventing radiographic damage than biologic monotherapy.

Classes of approved targeted therapies include: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab), IL-6 receptor inhibitors (tocilizumab, sarilumab), T-cell co-stimulation inhibitor (abatacept), B-cell depleting antibody (rituximab), and oral targeted synthetic JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib).

Prior to initiating any biologic or JAK inhibitor, mandatory screening includes testing for latent tuberculosis (IGRA or tuberculin skin test with chest radiograph) and chronic viral hepatitis B and C; active or untreated latent TB must receive prophylactic antimycobacterial therapy before commencing biologics.

The ORAL Surveillance trial in patients aged >=50 with cardiovascular risk factors demonstrated that the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib was associated with increased risks of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), venous thromboembolism (VTE), and malignancies compared with TNF inhibitors; regulatory agencies advise reserving JAK inhibitors for patients with inadequate response or contraindications to other therapies.

Rituximab (anti-CD20) is particularly efficacious in seropositive (RF-positive and/or ACPA-positive) RA, administered as two 1,000 mg IV infusions 14 days apart, but requires pre-treatment screening for hepatitis B (risk of fatal reactivation) and surveillance for secondary hypogammaglobulinemia.

uncertainties: Successful DMARD tapering and dose-reduction strategies in patients maintaining sustained deep clinical and ultrasound remission.
Long-term comparative malignancy risks among selective JAK-1 inhibitors versus pan-JAK inhibitors.
mcq_angles: Safety findings of ORAL Surveillance trial: JAK inhibitors carry black-box warnings for MACE, venous thromboembolism, and malignancies in older patients with CV risk.
Mandatory screening before starting TNF/JAK inhibitors: IGRA/chest X-ray for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc).
Biologic class of choice in seropositive RA after TNF failure: rituximab (anti-CD20) or tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R).

page.mentor_intro: Early diagnosis and immediate initiation of conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) within the 'window of opportunity' (<3 months from symptom onset) are critical to arrest synovial inflammation and prevent irreversible cartilage destruction and bone erosions in rheumatoid arthritis.

teaching_points.claim: Methotrexate (MTX) is the foundational, anchor first-line csDMARD for all active rheumatoid arthritis patients without contraindications, initiated at 10 to 15 mg weekly and rapidly escalated (by 5 mg every 2 to 4 weeks) to a target dose of 20 to 25 mg weekly orally or subcutaneously.

Concomitant oral folic acid (5 mg weekly or 1 mg daily except on the day of methotrexate) must be prescribed to reduce methotrexate-induced adverse effects, including oral stomatitis, nausea, transaminitis, and cytopenias, without diminishing therapeutic antirheumatic efficacy.

Subcutaneous methotrexate provides superior bioavailability, higher clinical response rates, and fewer gastrointestinal side effects compared with oral administration at doses >=15–20 mg weekly, serving as an effective step before declaring methotrexate treatment failure.

Short-term bridging glucocorticoids (low-dose oral prednisone <=10 mg daily or intramuscular/intra-articular depot methylprednisolone) provide rapid symptomatic relief during the 6- to 12-week latency period before csDMARDs achieve therapeutic efficacy, but must be tapered and discontinued as rapidly as clinically feasible.

Treat-to-Target (T2T) strategy mandates systematic objective assessment of disease activity (using CDAI, SDAI, or DAS28) every 1 to 3 months; if at least 50% improvement is not achieved by 3 months or target remission/low disease activity by 6 months, treatment adjustment (adding sulfasalazine/hydroxychloroquine or escalating to a biologic) is required.

uncertainties: Comparative long-term structural outcomes of initial csDMARD monotherapy versus upfront triple csDMARD therapy (methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine).
Role of baseline ultrasound-detected tenosynovitis and power Doppler positivity in selecting patients for upfront biologic DMARD initiation.
mcq_angles: Treat-to-target evaluation timeline: failure to achieve >=50% reduction in disease activity by 3 months or remission by 6 months mandates immediate DMARD escalation.
Folic acid co-prescription rule: weekly folic acid significantly reduces methotrexate gastrointestinal and hepatic toxicity without impairing DMARD efficacy.
Contraindications to methotrexate: pregnancy/breastfeeding (teratogen), severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min), chronic liver disease, and active alcohol abuse.

page.mentor_intro: Pulmonary involvement is the most common extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and a leading cause of RA-related mortality. Manifestations encompass interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD), pleural disease, pulmonary nodules, and airway disorders (bronchiectasis, bronchiolitis obliterans).

teaching_points.claim: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) affects 10–15% of RA patients clinically and up to 30% subclinically; unlike most other connective tissue diseases where NSIP predominates, RA-ILD characteristically exhibits an aggressive Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP) high-resolution CT pattern (subpleural basal reticulation, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis).

High-titer seropositivity (RF and anti-CCP / ACPA), male sex, older age, smoking history, and elevated disease activity scores are strong independent risk factors for the development and progression of RA-ILD.

In patients with progressive fibrosing interstitial lung disease despite immunosuppression, the landmark INBUILD trial established that the intracellular tyrosine kinase inhibitor nintedanib significantly reduces the annual rate of decline in forced vital capacity (FVC).

Immunosuppressive management of inflammatory RA-ILD incorporates corticosteroids combined with mycophenolate mofetil (preferred first-line), rituximab, or abatacept; in contrast, TNF inhibitors carry variable associations with ILD flare and should be used with caution.

Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are typically subpleural, well-circumscribed, and asymptomatic; they can cavitate, rupture causing secondary pneumothorax or pleural effusion (characteristically with very low pleural fluid glucose <1.6 mmol/L and high LDH), and can be accelerated by methotrexate therapy ('accelerated nodulosis').

uncertainties: Causal contribution of methotrexate to acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis versus progressive RA-ILD progression.
Comparative efficacy of rituximab versus mycophenolate mofetil as first-line induction therapy for rapidly progressive RA-ILD.
mcq_angles: Predominant HRCT pattern in RA-ILD: Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP) with basal subpleural honeycombing, contrasting with scleroderma and myositis (NSIP).
Pleural fluid signature of rheumatoid pleurisy: extremely low pleural fluid glucose (<1.6 mmol/L / <30 mg/dL), pH <7.20, and markedly elevated rheumatoid factor.
Antifibrotic indication in RA-ILD: nintedanib slows FVC decline in progressive fibrosing phenotype based on the INBUILD trial.

page.mentor_intro: Acute right ventricular (RV) failure in the intensive care unit is a hemodynamic emergency characterized by ventriculo-arterial uncoupling, systemic congestion, and low cardiac output. Effective management hinges on optimizing RV preload, reducing RV afterload, augmenting inotropy, and avoiding detrimental mechanical ventilation settings.

teaching_points.claim: Acute right ventricular failure is provoked by abrupt increases in RV afterload (massive pulmonary embolism, acute respiratory distress syndrome ARDS, severe hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) or primary RV ischemia/infarction; the thin-walled RV rapidly dilates, shifting the interventricular septum leftward ('D-shaped' left ventricle), impairing left ventricular diastolic filling and precipitating systemic hypotension.

Preload management requires avoiding fluid overload; while moderate initial volume expansion may benefit hypovolemic patients, excessive volume worsens RV wall tension, triggers tricuspid annular dilation with functional severe tricuspid regurgitation, and compromises LV stroke volume; central venous decongestion with loop diuretics or ultrafiltration is frequently required.

Maintaining adequate coronary perfusion pressure is paramount: the right coronary artery supplies the RV throughout both systole and diastole; systemic hypotension reduces RV myocardial perfusion, triggering ischemia and a fatal spiral of RV dilation; noradrenaline is the vasopressor of choice to restore systemic vascular resistance and aortic root pressure.

Targeted RV afterload reduction utilizes inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (inhaled nitric oxide [iNO] 10–40 ppm or inhaled prostacyclin [iloprost/epoprostenol]), which selectively dilate ventilated pulmonary vascular beds without causing systemic hypotension.

Mechanical ventilation in RV failure demands lung-protective strategies to avoid increasing pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR): hypercapnia, severe hypoxia, acidosis, high mean airway pressures, and excessive PEEP all dramatically elevate PVR; tidal volumes should be limited to 6 mL/kg PBW with driving pressure minimized.

uncertainties: Threshold and timing for percutaneous right ventricular mechanical circulatory support (e.g., Impella RP or ProtekDuo) in medical RV failure.
Optimal PEEP titration strategy balancing alveolar recruitment against pulmonary vascular resistance and RV afterload in ARDS-induced cor pulmonale.
mcq_angles: Hemodynamic goal in acute RV failure: maintain systemic MAP with noradrenaline to preserve right coronary artery perfusion pressure and prevent RV ischemic collapse.
Inhaled versus systemic pulmonary vasodilators: inhaled nitric oxide or epoprostenol selectively reduces pulmonary vascular resistance without systemic vasodilation.
Echocardiographic hallmark of RV pressure overload: McConnell sign (RV free wall hypokinesia with preserved apex sparing) and leftward septal flattening ('D-shaped' LV).

A 64-year-old mechanically ventilated man with severe ARDS whose echocardiogram shows acute RV dilation, TAPSE 10 mm, and severe tricuspid regurgitation.

page.mentor_intro: Rituximab depletes B cells and is used in rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis and lupus. Safe use needs hepatitis B and infection screening, premedication, and monitoring of immunoglobulin levels because hypogammaglobulinaemia can follow repeated courses.

teaching_points.claim: Before rituximab, check hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc), baseline immunoglobulins, and assess tuberculosis, HIV and hepatitis C risk; give antiviral prophylaxis if there is current or past hepatitis B exposure.
In rheumatoid arthritis, the standard regimen is 1,000 mg IV on days 1 and 15, with methylprednisolone 100 mg IV, paracetamol and an antihistamine as premedication.
IgG should be measured before each course; persistent hypogammaglobulinaemia (IgG below about 4 to 5 g/L) with recurrent serious infection warrants immunoglobulin replacement.
Live vaccines are avoided and inactivated vaccines should ideally be given before treatment because B-cell depletion blunts responses.

page.mentor_intro: The landmark JUPITER trial demonstrated that in apparently healthy adults with normal LDL cholesterol but elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP >= 2 mg/L), rosuvastatin 20 mg significantly reduced major cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality, establishing systemic inflammation as a treatable risk enhancer in primary prevention.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark JUPITER trial (Ridker et al., NEJM), rosuvastatin (20 mg daily) significantly reduced the primary composite endpoint of myocardial infarction, stroke, arterial revascularization, hospitalization for unstable angina, or death from cardiovascular causes by 44% (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.46-0.69) in individuals with LDL-C <130 mg/dL and hsCRP >=2.0 mg/dL.

Rosuvastatin therapy resulted in a median reduction in LDL cholesterol of 50% (down to 55 mg/dL) and a median reduction in hsCRP of 37% (down to 2.2 mg/L) at 12 months, demonstrating simultaneous profound lipid and inflammatory suppression.

JUPITER demonstrated a significant 20% reduction in all-cause mortality (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.67-0.97, P=0.02) without significant increases in myopathy or cancer, leading to trial termination at a median follow-up of 1.9 years due to unequivocal efficacy.

Contemporary multi-society cholesterol guidelines recognize persistently elevated hsCRP (>=2.0 mg/dL) as a validated risk-enhancing factor supporting the initiation or intensification of statin therapy in intermediate-risk primary prevention, while monitoring for a small absolute increase in physician-reported incident diabetes.

page.mentor_intro: The angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) sacubitril/valsartan is a cornerstone guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Simultaneous neprilysin inhibition and angiotensin receptor blockade enhance natriuretic peptide signaling while counteracting neurohormonal maladaptation.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial of patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, LVEF <=40%), sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced the composite endpoint of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization by 20% compared with enalapril (HR 0.80, P<0.001).

Transitioning from an ACE inhibitor to sacubitril/valsartan requires a mandatory 36-hour washout period to prevent bradykinin accumulation and the life-threatening risk of angioedema; this washout is not required when switching from an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB).

Sacubitril degrades neprilysin, preventing breakdown of natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP, CNP), bradykinin, and adrenomedullin; consequently, plasma B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels increase during therapy, making N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP)—which is not a neprilysin substrate—the only reliable biomarker for monitoring.

Target maintenance dosing is 97/103 mg twice daily (equivalent to 200 mg twice daily); titration from initial lower doses (24/26 mg or 49/51 mg twice daily) is performed every 2 to 4 weeks while monitoring blood pressure, serum potassium, and renal function.

uncertainties: Safety and efficacy of in-hospital ARNI initiation immediately following hemodynamic stabilization from acute decompensated heart failure (PIONEER-HF).
Long-term cognitive safety profile regarding neprilysin-mediated degradation of amyloid-beta in the central nervous system.
mcq_angles: Mandatory washout rule: strict 36-hour drug-free interval between last ACE inhibitor dose and first ARNI dose to prevent fatal angioedema.
Biomarker interpretation on ARNI: BNP rises due to neprilysin inhibition; NT-proBNP must be measured to evaluate clinical congestion and treatment response.
Guideline-directed 4-pillar HFrEF therapy: ARNI, evidence-based beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA), and SGLT2 inhibitor.

page.mentor_intro: Pulmonary sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder of unknown etiology, characterized pathologically by non-caseating epithelioid granulomas. Clinical presentation ranges from incidental asymptomatic bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy to progressive pulmonary fibrosis and respiratory failure.

teaching_points.claim: Pathological hallmark of sarcoidosis is the presence of well-formed, non-caseating epithelioid granulomas composed of CD4+ T helper cells, epithelioid histiocytes, and multinucleated giant cells (often containing Schaumann bodies and asteroid bodies); special stains and cultures must strictly exclude mycobacterial and fungal infections.

Chest radiographic staging (Scadding criteria) categorizes pulmonary involvement into: Stage 0 (normal radiograph), Stage I (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy [BHL] alone), Stage II (BHL plus parenchymal pulmonary infiltration), Stage III (parenchymal infiltration without BHL), and Stage IV (end-stage pulmonary fibrosis, predominantly upper-lobe reticulation, volume loss, and traction bronchiectasis).

Lofgren syndrome—the acute, benign presentation combining bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, bilateral ankle periarthritis, and fever—has an >80–90% spontaneous remission rate within 1 to 2 years and typically requires only supportive NSAID therapy rather than systemic corticosteroids.

High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest characteristically demonstrates a perilymphatic distribution of micronodules along bronchovascular bundles, subpleural surfaces, and interlobular septa, predominantly affecting middle and upper lung zones.

Diagnostic tissue confirmation is achieved via endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) of mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes, which provides superior diagnostic yield (>85–90%) and lower complication rates compared with transbronchial lung biopsy.

uncertainties: Prognostic reliability of serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R) compared to serum ACE in predicting disease progression.
Optimal threshold and criteria for initiating antifibrotic therapy in Stage IV fibrotic sarcoidosis with progressive lung functional decline.
mcq_angles: Scadding radiographic stages: Stage I = bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy alone; Stage II = BHL + parenchymal infiltrates; Stage IV = pulmonary fibrosis with upper-lobe volume loss.
Lofgren syndrome features and prognosis: erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, arthritis/fever; carries excellent prognosis and high spontaneous resolution.
Histological requirement: non-caseating granulomas with negative acid-fast bacilli and fungal stains to exclude tuberculosis and histoplasmosis.

page.mentor_intro: Systemic immunosuppression in sarcoidosis is reserved for organ- or life-threatening disease, or debilitating symptoms impairing quality of life. Oral corticosteroids remain the first-line therapy, with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants and targeted TNF inhibitors utilized for chronic, progressive, or steroid-refractory disease.

teaching_points.claim: Absolute indications for systemic immunosuppressive therapy in sarcoidosis include cardiac sarcoidosis, central nervous system involvement (neurosarcoidosis), sight-threatening ocular disease, hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria with nephrocalcinosis, and progressive pulmonary functional decline.

Oral corticosteroids (prednisone 20 to 40 mg daily / 0.5 mg/kg) are the established first-line treatment; clinical and functional response is assessed at 3 to 6 months, followed by gradual dose tapering to the lowest effective dose (<=5–10 mg daily) or discontinuation over 6 to 12 months.

Second-line steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agents—methotrexate (preferred, 10–20 mg weekly with folic acid), azathioprine (1.5–2.5 mg/kg daily), or leflunomide—are indicated when patients experience corticosteroid toxicity, require >10 mg/day prednisone to maintain remission, or fail to respond to steroids.

For refractory or progressive disease, third-line therapy with TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab 5 mg/kg IV or adalimumab) demonstrates proven efficacy in closing lupus pernio lesions, suppressing neurosarcoidosis, and arresting refractory pulmonary disease.

Abnormal vitamin D metabolism in sarcoidosis is driven by 1-alpha-hydroxylase expression in activated macrophages inside granulomas, producing excessive 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol); this causes intestinal hyperabsorption of calcium, hypercalciuria, and hypercalcemia, which responds promptly to corticosteroid suppression.

uncertainties: Optimal duration of infliximab maintenance therapy in neurosarcoidosis and relapse rates following biologic withdrawal.
Role of JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib) in cutaneous and multi-organ recalcitrant sarcoidosis.
mcq_angles: Mechanism of hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis: macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase overexpression inside granulomas produces autonomous 1,25(OH)2D (calcitriol) independent of PTH.

Third-line targeted biologic therapy: infliximab (monoclonal anti-TNF-alpha) is the evidence-based biologic of choice for refractory sarcoidosis.

page.mentor_intro: Scabies is a contagious parasitic skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. Transmission occurs through prolonged direct skin-to-skin contact, producing intense nocturnal pruritus and characteristic burrows. Effective eradication demands simultaneous treatment of all household contacts.

teaching_points.claim: Classic scabies is caused by female mites burrowing into the stratum corneum to lay eggs, eliciting a Type IV hypersensitivity allergic reaction that manifests 3 to 6 weeks after primary infestation (or 1 to 4 days upon re-infestation) with intense, debilitating nocturnal pruritus.

Pathognomonic physical examination findings are linear or serpiginous burrows, most frequently located in web spaces of fingers, flexor wrists, axillae, umbilicus, belt line, buttocks, and male genitalia (penile and scrotal papules/nodules); the head and neck are classically spared in adults but can be involved in infants and older adults.

First-line topical therapy is 5% permethrin dermal cream applied from neck to toes (including scalp/face in infants/elderly), left on for 8 to 14 hours before washing off, and repeated in 7 to 14 days to eradicate newly hatched nymphs.

Oral ivermectin (200 ug/kg taken as two single doses spaced 7 to 14 days apart) is equally efficacious to topical permethrin and represents the treatment of choice for institutional outbreaks, crusted scabies, and patients with poor compliance or severe eczema.

Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is a severe, hyperkeratotic variant occurring in immunosuppressed, neurologically impaired, or elderly individuals, characterized by thick scaly crusts harboring millions of mites; it is highly contagious through fomites and requires combination therapy (repeated oral ivermectin plus daily 5% permethrin) and strict contact isolation.

uncertainties: Emergence of clinical permethrin resistance in widespread community outbreaks and optimal timing for switching to oral ivermectin.
Safety and dosing protocols for oral ivermectin in pregnant women and infants weighing under 15 kg.
mcq_angles: Treatment schedule rule: any scabicide regimen (topical permethrin or oral ivermectin) MUST be repeated 7 to 14 days later because treatments do not kill unhatched eggs.
Mandatory epidemiological rule: all household members, sexual contacts, and close personal contacts must be treated simultaneously, regardless of whether symptoms are present.
Post-scabetic pruritus: persistent itching for 2 to 4 weeks after successful mite eradication is common due to residual mite antigens and does NOT indicate treatment failure.

page.mentor_intro: Schistosomiasis is a trematode infection acquired from freshwater; praziquantel is the drug of choice. Species determine the organ pattern: urinary for S. haematobium, hepatosplenic for S. mansoni and japonicum.

teaching_points.claim: Praziquantel is effective against all schistosome species; typical dosing is 40 mg/kg (S. mansoni, S. haematobium) and 60 mg/kg (S. japonicum) in divided doses, repeated after 4 to 6 weeks in travellers because it does not kill immature worms.
S. haematobium causes terminal haematuria, bladder wall calcification, hydronephrosis, and raises the risk of bladder squamous cell carcinoma.
S. mansoni and S. japonicum cause periportal (Symmers pipestem) fibrosis with presinusoidal portal hypertension, splenomegaly and variceal bleeding with preserved liver synthetic function.
Albendazole (400 mg single dose) treats soil-transmitted helminths such as Ascaris, hookworm and Trichuris.
Tropical (hyperreactive malarial) splenomegaly is massive splenomegaly with high IgM in malaria-endemic areas, managed with long-term antimalarial prophylaxis.

page.mentor_intro: Antipsychotic pharmacotherapy is the cornerstone of treatment for schizophrenia, effectively reducing positive psychotic symptoms and preventing relapses. Selecting between first- and second-generation agents balances therapeutic efficacy against neurological, metabolic, and cardiovascular side-effect profiles.

teaching_points.claim: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics (e.g., aripiprazole, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine) are guideline-preferred first-line options due to a lower risk of extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and tardive dyskinesia compared with first-generation (typical) high-potency antipsychotics (haloperidol).

Second-generation agents carry substantial cardiometabolic risks (weight gain, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes), with olanzapine and clozapine carrying the highest risk, and aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone carrying the lowest metabolic liability; baseline and regular metabolic monitoring (weight, fasting glucose, lipid panel) is mandatory.

Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS)—defined as persistent moderate-to-severe symptoms despite adequate trials of at least two different antipsychotics (at therapeutic doses for >=6 weeks, with at least one being a second-generation agent)—is an absolute indication for clozapine.

Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with proven superiority in treatment-resistant schizophrenia and reducing suicidal behavior; however, it requires strict hematological monitoring due to the risk of life-threatening severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis (absolute neutrophil count ANC cutoff: withhold if ANC <1,500/uL / <1.5 x 10^9/L, or <1,000/uL in benign ethnic neutropenia).

Long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics (e.g., paliperidone palmitate, aripiprazole lauroxil, haloperidol decanoate) significantly reduce hospital readmissions and relapse rates in patients with poor medication adherence or frequent relapses, and should be offered early in the illness course.

uncertainties: Role of adjunctive glutamate-modulating agents (e.g., NMDA receptor modulators) in treating persistent negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia.
Optimal timing for introducing long-acting injectable formulations following the first psychotic episode.
mcq_angles: Indication for clozapine: treatment-resistant schizophrenia following two failed antipsychotic trials; clozapine significantly reduces all-cause mortality and suicide risk.
Clozapine monitoring parameters: mandatory regular absolute neutrophil count (ANC) monitoring to detect agranulocytosis; other lethal risks include myocarditis and severe constipation/ileus.
Metabolic liability spectrum: olanzapine and clozapine cause the greatest weight gain and metabolic syndrome; aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone are metabolically neutral.

page.mentor_intro: Schnitzler Syndrome is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

teaching_points.claim: Systematic review evidence supports protocolized evaluation and targeted therapeutic intervention: Schnitzler syndrome without monoclonal gammopathy: a systematic review and case presentation.

Schnitzler syndrome is a rare autoinflammatory disorder characterized by a chronic urticarial exanthem and monoclonal IgM (rarely IgG) gammopathy, accompanied by recurrent fevers, bone pain, leukocytosis, and systemic inflammation; targeted interleukin-1 receptor antagonism with anakinra or canakinumab produces rapid, complete clinical and biochemical remission, confirming its IL-1-driven pathogenesis.

Diagnostic criteria (Lipsker or Strasbourg criteria) require chronic urticaria and monoclonal IgM (or IgG) plus at least two minor criteria: recurrent fever, leukocytosis, bone pain/hyperostosis, or elevated acute-phase reactants.
IL-1 receptor antagonist therapy (anakinra 100 mg daily subcutaneously) achieves rapid resolution of fever and urticaria within 24 to 48 hours and normalizes inflammatory markers in >90% of patients.

page.mentor_intro: Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) is a life-threatening complication of systemic sclerosis, primarily affecting patients with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and RNA polymerase III antibodies. Characterized by abrupt, severe hypertension, acute oliguric renal failure, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, SRC is a medical emergency.

teaching_points.claim: Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) occurs in 5–15% of patients with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc), strongly associated with anti-RNA polymerase III antibody seropositivity, rapid progression of skin thickening, and recent high-dose corticosteroid exposure (prednisone >=15 mg/day).

The classic clinical presentation is an abrupt onset of severe 'flash' hypertension (systolic BP >160–180 mmHg or diastolic >100 mmHg), progressive oliguric acute kidney injury, mild proteinuria, microscopic hematuria with granular casts, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA with thrombocytopenia and schistocytes on blood smear).

Approximately 10–15% of SRC cases are 'normotensive' (normotensive scleroderma renal crisis), which carries a significantly worse renal prognosis and higher mortality due to delayed clinical recognition.

Immediate initiation of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitors—specifically short-acting oral captopril—is the definitive, life-saving therapy; captopril reverses intrarenal vasoconstriction, lowers mortality from >90% to <30%, and should be aggressively up-titrated to normalize blood pressure within 48 to 72 hours.

ACE inhibitors must be maintained even if serum creatinine initially rises during acute blood pressure lowering; prophylactic use of ACE inhibitors prior to SRC onset is ineffective and associated with worse outcomes, while high-dose systemic corticosteroids are strictly contraindicated as they precipitate SRC.

uncertainties: Efficacy of adjunctive terminal complement C5 inhibition (eculizumab) in patients with SRC-induced thrombotic microangiopathy refractory to ACE inhibitors.
Threshold and timing for initiating renal replacement therapy with prospective expectation of delayed renal recovery up to 12 to 24 months.
mcq_angles: Medication that precipitates SRC: systemic glucocorticoids (prednisone >=15 mg/day) are strongly associated with triggering scleroderma renal crisis.
Drug of choice for SRC: prompt initiation and aggressive titration of oral captopril (ACE inhibitor); do not substitute with ARBs as first-line.
Antibody profile linked to highest SRC risk: anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies carry the highest risk among scleroderma-specific autoantibodies.

page.mentor_intro: The management of scleroderma renal crisis represents a true hypertensive emergency where prompt pharmacological intervention with short-acting ACE inhibitors dictates survival. Careful hemodynamic titration preserves renal perfusion while arresting hyperreninemic cortical ischemia.

teaching_points.claim: Scleroderma renal crisis is driven by intense renal cortical vasospasm and intimal arterial proliferation ('onion-skin' hypertrophy), resulting in severe renal hypoperfusion and massive activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (hyperreninemic state).

Short-acting oral captopril is the gold-standard agent of choice, initiated at a low test dose (6.25 to 12.5 mg) and rapidly escalated every 4 to 8 hours up to maximum doses (50–100 mg three times daily) to achieve a target reduction in systolic blood pressure of approx. 20 mmHg per 24 hours.

Blood pressure lowering should be controlled and gradual, aiming for normalization (systolic BP 120–130 mmHg) over 48 to 72 hours; overly rapid precipitous drops in blood pressure can exacerbate renal cortical hypoperfusion and precipitate acute tubular necrosis.

If blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite maximal ACE inhibitor titration, second-line add-on antihypertensives include dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nicardipine) or intravenous prostacyclin analogues (iloprost); beta-blockers and ARBs are avoided as first-line adjuncts.

Renal recovery is characteristically slow and may occur up to 12 to 24 months following the acute episode; approximately 50% of patients requiring temporary hemodialysis can successfully discontinue dialysis if ACE inhibitors are continuously maintained.

uncertainties: Comparative safety and pharmacokinetic stability of long-acting ACE inhibitors (enalapril, ramipril) once initial stabilization is achieved with captopril.
Role of endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan) in mitigating chronic vascular remodeling following acute scleroderma renal crisis.
mcq_angles: Target blood pressure lowering rate: reduce systolic BP by approx. 20 mmHg/day, achieving normal BP over 48-72 hours to prevent ischemic acute tubular necrosis.
Persistence of dialysis dependence: over 50% of patients who initially require dialysis during SRC achieve renal recovery and come off dialysis within 1-2 years if ACEi is continued.
Second-line antihypertensive agent of choice: calcium channel blockers (e.g. amlodipine, nicardipine) or intravenous prostacyclins added to maximal captopril.

teaching_points.claim: Contemporary evidence synthesis highlights core pathophysiology, clinical staging, and multidisciplinary management: Secondary headaches - red and green flags and their significance for diagnostics.

The SNOOP4 mnemonic (Systemic symptoms/fever, Neurological deficits, Onset sudden/thunderclap, Older age >50, Pattern change/Positional/Papilledema) identifies high-risk red flags requiring urgent neuroimaging; thunderclap headaches mandate immediate non-contrast cranial CT followed by lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if CT is negative within 6 hours to definitively exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Positional headaches that worsen when upright and improve when recumbent indicate spontaneous intracranial hypotension (CSF leak), whereas headaches worsening when supine or with Valsalva indicate elevated intracranial pressure.

In patients over 50 presenting with new-onset headache, temporal artery tenderness, scalp tenderness, or jaw claudication, immediate erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), CRP, and high-dose systemic steroids are required to prevent visual loss from giant cell arteritis.

page.mentor_intro: Secondary immunodeficiency (SID) is increasingly recognized in patients receiving long-term systemic corticosteroids, immunosuppressive therapies, and targeted biologics. Understanding drug-specific immunosuppressive mechanisms enables proactive risk stratification, targeted antimicrobial prophylaxis, and monitoring for hypogammaglobulinemia.

teaching_points.claim: Systemic corticosteroids impair cellular immunity, phagocyte function, and cytokine expression in a dose- and duration-dependent manner; chronic prednisone doses >=15–20 mg/day (or cumulative doses >700 mg) significantly increase the risk of opportunistic infections, predominantly Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), Aspergillus, and reactivation of latent tuberculosis.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX, 1 single-strength tablet daily or 1 double-strength tablet 3 times weekly) is strongly indicated for patients receiving prednisone >=15–20 mg daily for >=4 weeks in combination with a second immunosuppressive agent.

B-cell depleting therapies (rituximab, obinutuzumab) cause prolonged peripheral B-cell aplasia and can induce progressive, symptomatic secondary hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG <4–5 g/L), resulting in recurrent encapsulated sinopulmonary bacterial infections; baseline and serial quantitative immunoglobulin (IgG, IgA, IgM) monitoring is mandatory.

TNF-alpha inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab) selectively impair granuloma maintenance and macrophage activation, markedly increasing the risk of active tuberculosis reactivation (often presenting with atypical, extrapulmonary, or disseminated disease) and intracellular infections (Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Listeria).

In patients with severe secondary hypogammaglobulinemia (serum IgG <4.0 g/L) and recurrent or severe bacterial infections despite antibiotic prophylaxis, immunoglobulin replacement therapy (IVIG or SCIG) significantly reduces pneumonia rates and hospitalization.

uncertainties: Threshold criteria of serum IgG level versus clinical infection frequency for initiating replacement IVIG/SCIG in secondary hypogammaglobulinemia.
Vaccination response kinetics and optimal scheduling of non-live vaccines relative to B-cell reconstitution following rituximab therapy.

Rituximab long-term complication: secondary hypogammaglobulinemia (low IgG) leading to recurrent bacterial respiratory tract infections, requiring quantitative IgG monitoring.
Infection pattern with TNF inhibitors: breakdown of granulomas leading to disseminated or extrapulmonary tuberculosis and endemic mycoses (histoplasmosis).

page.mentor_intro: Secondary (functional) mitral regurgitation (SMR) arises from left ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction rather than structural valvular disease. The landmark COAPT trial established that transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) with the MitraClip system provides substantial mortality and hospitalization benefits in appropriately selected heart failure patients.

teaching_points.claim: Secondary mitral regurgitation (SMR) is a disease of the left ventricle: LV enlargement and regional wall motion abnormalities displace papillary muscles, causing tethering and restricted leaflet motion (Carpentier Type IIIb) and failure of coaptation across a structurally normal mitral valve.

Optimal Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT)—including the four foundational pillars (ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) if indicated—is the mandatory first-line strategy, which frequently promotes reverse LV remodeling and reduces SMR severity.

The landmark COAPT randomized trial demonstrated that transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER with MitraClip) added to maximal GDMT in patients with symptomatic heart failure and severe SMR significantly reduced heart failure hospitalizations by 47% (HR 0.53, P<0.001) and all-cause mortality by 38% (HR 0.62, P<0.001) at 2 and 5 years.

Discrepancy with the neutral MITRA-FR trial is explained by the concept of 'disproportionate' versus 'proportionate' mitral regurgitation: COAPT enrolled patients with severe MR (effective regurgitant orifice area EROA >=30-40 mm2) relative to moderate LV dilation (LV end-systolic dimension LVESD <=70 mm), whereas MITRA-FR enrolled patients with more extreme LV dilation and less severe MR.

Patient eligibility criteria for MitraClip TEER in secondary MR require persistent symptomatic NYHA class II-IV heart failure despite maximal GDMT, LVEF between 20% and 50%, LVESD <=70 mm, pulmonary artery systolic pressure <=70 mmHg, and favorable transesophageal echocardiographic anatomy.

uncertainties: Long-term clinical durability of transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) versus transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) in secondary MR.
Management of persistent mild-to-moderate residual mitral regurgitation following single or dual clip deployment.
mcq_angles: COAPT trial landmark outcome: MitraClip TEER added to GDMT significantly reduces 2-year all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalizations in disproportionate severe SMR.
Why COAPT succeeded and MITRA-FR did not: COAPT selected patients with truly severe SMR (EROA >=30 mm2) without end-stage extreme LV dilation (LVESD <=70 mm).
Mandatory first step before MitraClip consideration: maximal optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and CRT for at least 3 months.
case_hooks: A 66-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%, LVESD 58 mm) on maximal GDMT with persistent NYHA Class III dyspnea and severe functional MR (EROA 42 mm2).
A 72-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 15%, LVESD 76 mm) evaluated for MitraClip whose extreme ventriculomegaly reflects proportionate end-stage cardiomyopathy.

page.mentor_intro: Secondary stroke prevention requires tailoring antithrombotic therapy to the underlying stroke mechanism. Antiplatelet therapy is standard for non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke and TIA, whereas therapeutic anticoagulation is mandatory for cardioembolic stroke, predominantly atrial fibrillation.

teaching_points.claim: For non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke and high-risk TIA (ABCD2 score >=4 or minor stroke with NIHSS <=3), urgent dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin (150-300 mg loading, then 75-100 mg daily) plus clopidogrel (300-600 mg loading, then 75 mg daily) initiated within 24 hours and continued for 21 days (CHANCE and POINT trials) significantly reduces recurrent stroke risk without excess major hemorrhage.

In patients with minor stroke or TIA and confirmed intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (ICAS >=70%), the THALES trial demonstrated that DAPT with aspirin plus ticagrelor (90 mg twice daily for 30 days) significantly reduces stroke recurrence or death compared with aspirin alone.

For long-term maintenance monotherapy beyond 21 to 30 days, single antiplatelet therapy with clopidogrel (75 mg daily) or aspirin (75-100 mg daily) is recommended; long-term DAPT beyond 90 days carries an unacceptable risk of major intracranial and gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

For cardioembolic ischemic stroke secondary to non-valvular atrial fibrillation, Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) are superior to warfarin, achieving equivalent or lower ischemic stroke rates with a ~50% reduction in life-threatening intracranial hemorrhage.

Timing of anticoagulation initiation after acute cardioembolic stroke follows the '1-3-6-12 day rule' (or recent ELAN trial evidence supporting early initiation): day 1 for TIA, day 3-4 for minor stroke, day 6-7 for moderate stroke, and day 12-14 for large infarcts after repeat CT/MRI excludes hemorrhagic transformation.

uncertainties: Utility of CYP2C19 loss-of-function loss allele pharmacogenetic testing to guide clopidogrel versus ticagrelor selection in acute DAPT.
Efficacy and safety of direct oral Factor XIa inhibitors (e.g., asundexian, milvexian) in acute non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke prevention.
mcq_angles: Duration of short-term DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel): exactly 21 days for high-risk TIA or minor ischemic stroke (CHANCE/POINT trials), transitioning to monotherapy.
DOAC superiority over warfarin in AF stroke prevention: DOACs cause significantly lower rates of hemorrhagic stroke and intracranial hemorrhage.
Antiplatelets versus anticoagulants in non-cardioembolic stroke: anticoagulation provides no benefit over antiplatelet therapy for non-cardioembolic stroke and causes excess hemorrhage.

page.mentor_intro: Sedation and analgesia in critically ill mechanically ventilated adults are guided by the PADIS (Pain, Agitation/Sedation, Delirium, Immobility, and Sleep Disruption) clinical practice guidelines. Implementing the evidence-based ABCDEF bundle improves survival, accelerates weaning, and diminishes delirium.

teaching_points.claim: The PADIS guidelines prioritize an 'analgesia-first' (analgosedation) approach: pain assessment and intravenous opioid titration (fentanyl, morphine, hydromorphone) must precede the administration of sedative agents, as unmanaged pain is the leading trigger of ICU agitation.

Light sedation targets (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale [RASS] score -1 to 0) are strongly recommended over deep sedation; light sedation significantly reduces mechanical ventilation duration, ICU length of stay, and 90-day mortality without increasing accidental extubation.

Non-benzodiazepine sedatives—specifically propofol and the selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist dexmedetomidine—are preferred over benzodiazepines (midazolam, lorazepam), which are independent risk factors for prolonged ventilation, delirium, and cognitive impairment.

The evidence-based ABCDEF bundle integrates multidisciplinary care: Assess/prevent/manage pain (A), Both Spontaneous Awakening Trials and Spontaneous Breathing Trials (B), Choice of analgesia and sedation (C), Delirium assessment/prevention/management using CAM-ICU (D), Early mobility and exercise (E), and Family engagement and empowerment (F).

Routine screening for delirium using validated tools (Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU [CAM-ICU] or Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist [ICDSC]) is mandatory; non-pharmacological interventions (reorientation, day-night circadian light cycles, noise reduction, early mobilization) are first-line, while routine prophylactic antipsychotics (haloperidol) do not reduce delirium incidence or mortality.

uncertainties: Optimal role and timing of volatile anesthetic sedation (isoflurane/sevoflurane delivered via Anaconda/Sedaconda devices) in long-term ICU sedation.
Comparative delirium and hemodynamic outcomes of dexmedetomidine versus propofol in patients with severe septic shock.
mcq_angles: Sedative choice in ICU: propofol or dexmedetomidine preferred over benzodiazepines (midazolam) due to lower delirium and faster extubation.
Target RASS score: aim for light sedation (RASS -1 to 0: drowsy to alert and calm) rather than deep sedation (RASS -3 to -5).
ABCDEF bundle components: paired daily Spontaneous Awakening Trial (SAT) and Spontaneous Breathing Trial (SBT) accelerate liberation from mechanical ventilation.

A 68-year-old woman in the ICU who becomes acutely confused, inattentive, and agitated on postoperative day 2 following cardiac surgery with a positive CAM-ICU.

page.mentor_intro: Procedural sedation outside the operating theater requires rigorous pre-procedural risk assessment, standardized physiological monitoring, and immediate access to airway rescue equipment. Maintaining safety hinges on recognizing sedation depths, adherence to fasting guidelines, and prompt reversal of over-sedation.

teaching_points.claim: Procedural sedation outside the operating room requires dedicated pre-procedure fasting assessment (typically 2 hours for clear fluids, 6 hours for light meals), continuous multi-parameter monitoring (pulse oximetry, continuous capnography, non-invasive blood pressure, ECG), and an independent trained practitioner whose sole responsibility is patient monitoring.

Continuous end-tidal CO2 capnography is mandatory for moderate and deep sedation because it detects hypoventilation, respiratory depression, and airway obstruction significantly earlier than pulse oximetry or visual inspection.

Specific pharmacological reversal agents must be immediately accessible: naloxone (0.1-0.2 mg titrated IV every 2-3 minutes) for opioid-induced respiratory depression, and flumazenil (0.2 mg IV titrated up to 1.0 mg) for benzodiazepine toxicity.

Propofol and dexmedetomidine provide rapid-onset, titratable sedation but lack specific pharmacological antagonists, necessitating direct supervision by clinicians skilled in advanced airway management and bag-mask ventilation.

uncertainties: Role of routine pre-procedure gastric point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) versus strict fasting hour intervals in emergency procedural sedation.
Safety profile of ketofol (ketamine-propofol combination) versus propofol monotherapy regarding hemodynamic stability and recovery time.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic superiority of capnography: capnography detects alveolar hypoventilation and apnea minutes before pulse oximetry desaturation, especially in supplemental oxygen.
Half-life hazard of reversal agents: naloxone and flumazenil have shorter half-lives than long-acting opioids/benzodiazepines, risking resedation.
Fasting guidelines for elective sedation: 2 hours for clears, 6 hours for solids, with emergency procedures balanced against aspiration risk.

page.mentor_intro: Valproate carries the greatest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of the antiseizure medicines and is avoided in women of childbearing potential where possible. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam carry the lowest risk, and folic acid is given before conception.

teaching_points.claim: Sodium valproate has the highest dose-dependent risk of major malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders; it should not be used in women of childbearing potential unless no alternative works and a pregnancy prevention programme is followed.
Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have the lowest recorded teratogenic risk; lamotrigine levels fall markedly in pregnancy through increased glucuronidation, so levels are monitored and doses adjusted.
UK guidance (NICE) advises folic acid 5 mg daily from before conception through the first trimester for all women with epilepsy; other bodies suggest lower doses, and evidence of benefit is limited.
Never stop antiseizure medication abruptly in pregnancy; uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures pose a greater risk to mother and fetus.

page.mentor_intro: Clinical assessment and management of self-harm and suicide risk requires a compassionate, non-judgmental, person-centered approach. Evidence-based suicide risk formulation prioritizes structured clinical assessment and collaborative safety planning over simplistic, unvalidated risk categorization scales.

teaching_points.claim: Standardized risk assessment scales (such as the SAD PERSONS scale) have very poor predictive validity (high false-positive and false-negative rates) and must never be used in isolation to determine hospital admission, discharge, or risk level; guidelines (NICE, APA) mandate a comprehensive psychosocial and clinical risk assessment.

Comprehensive suicide risk formulation identifies modifiable risk factors (active depression, psychosis, substance intoxication, access to lethal means, acute severe psychosocial stressors) and protective factors (social connectedness, children at home, future orientation, therapeutic alliance).

High-risk clinical indicators of suicidal intent include violent or highly lethal methods, meticulous planning and preparation (writing suicide notes, making wills, giving away possessions), active steps to avoid discovery, expressions of profound hopelessness, and persistent regret over surviving a suicide attempt.

Collaborative safety planning—co-creating a structured written Safety Planning Intervention (SPI) identifying personal warning signs, internal coping strategies, social distractions, trusted contacts, and emergency crisis lines—significantly reduces suicidal behavior and repeat presentations.

Restriction of access to lethal means (safe storage or disposal of firearms, lethal medications, poisons, and ligature points) is the single most effective public health and clinical intervention for reducing completed suicides.

In patients presenting with acute toxic ingestion or overdose, medical stabilization and poison control consultation (assessing acetaminophen levels, ECG for QRS/QTc prolongation) takes immediate priority alongside constant direct visual observation to ensure safety.

uncertainties: Predictive accuracy and clinical integration of machine learning algorithms analyzing electronic health records for emergent suicidal behavior.
Rapid antisuicidal efficacy and long-term durability of sub-anesthetic intravenous ketamine or intranasal esketamine in acute depressive crises.
mcq_angles: Predictive validity of risk assessment tools: structured numerical scales (e.g. SAD PERSONS) should not be used to predict suicide risk or determine admission due to low accuracy.
Most effective evidence-based suicide prevention strategy: restriction of access to lethal means (securing firearms, prescription medications).
Collaborative Safety Planning Intervention: structured six-step written personalized crisis plan reduces subsequent suicidal behavior.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark STEP 1 randomized trial of adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes, once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg combined with lifestyle intervention achieved a mean body weight reduction of -14.9% at 68 weeks versus -2.4% with placebo (treatment difference -12.4 percentage points, P<0.001).

page.mentor_intro: Sepsis is defined by the Sepsis-3 consensus as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock represents a severe subset with profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities carrying hospital mortality greater than 40%. Rapid bundle resuscitation is life-saving.

teaching_points.claim: According to the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3), sepsis is defined as an acute increase in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of >=2 points attributable to infection; septic shock is clinically identified by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP >=65 mmHg and a serum lactate >2.0 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) 1-hour bundle mandates immediate actions upon recognition: measure blood lactate (remeasure if initial lactate >2 mmol/L), obtain blood cultures prior to administering broad-spectrum antimicrobials, administer empiric broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials within 1 hour, and initiate rapid fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloids) for hypotension or lactate >=4 mmol/L.

Balanced crystalloids (Plasma-Lyte, Ringer's lactate) are preferred over 0.9% normal saline for fluid resuscitation, as large-volume saline causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and increases the incidence of acute kidney injury and renal replacement therapy.

Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) is the first-line vasopressor of choice, targeting a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of >=65 mmHg; vasopressin (titrated up to fixed 0.03 units/min) should be added as a second-line vasopressor if noradrenaline dose is escalating, while adrenaline is added if MAP remains refractory.

Low-dose intravenous corticosteroids (hydrocortisone 200 mg daily administered as 50 mg IV every 6 hours or continuous infusion) are indicated for patients with septic shock who have ongoing requirement for vasopressor therapy (noradrenaline or adrenaline >=0.25 ug/kg/min) for at least 4 hours.

Source control is an absolute emergency principle: identifying and intervening on anatomical infection foci (draining abscesses, debriding necrotizing soft-tissue infections, removing infected central venous catheters, relieving obstructed pyelonephritis) must be achieved within 6 to 12 hours.

uncertainties: Optimal fluid volume in patients with preexisting heart failure or end-stage renal disease (restrictive vs liberal 30 mL/kg fluid administration).
Role of hemoperfusion and extracorporeal cytokine adsorption cartridges (e.g., CytoSorb) in refractory hyperinflammatory septic shock.
mcq_angles: Sepsis-3 diagnostic criteria: SOFA score increase >=2 points represents sepsis; septic shock requires vasopressor dependency (MAP >=65 mmHg) AND lactate >2.0 mmol/L despite fluid repletion.
Fluid resuscitation choice: balanced crystalloids (Ringer's lactate) preferred over 0.9% saline to prevent hyperchloremic acidosis and acute kidney injury.
Indication for hydrocortisone: septic shock requiring escalating doses of vasopressors (noradrenaline >=0.25 ug/kg/min) for >4 hours.
case_hooks: A 68-year-old woman presenting with high fever, confusion, blood pressure 76/42 mmHg, heart rate 124 bpm, and serum lactate 4.8 mmol/L secondary to severe pyelonephritis.
A 52-year-old man in the ICU with perforated diverticulitis requiring noradrenaline 0.35 ug/kg/min and vasopressin 0.03 units/min to maintain a MAP of 65 mmHg.

page.mentor_intro: The Sepsis-3 consensus redefines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Identifying organ dysfunction via the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score and rapid delivery of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 1-hour resuscitation bundle are fundamental to improving survival.

teaching_points.claim: Under Sepsis-3, sepsis is defined as an acute increase in the total Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of >=2 points reflecting acute infection-induced multi-organ dysfunction (respiratory PaO2/FiO2, coagulation platelets, liver bilirubin, cardiovascular MAP/vasopressors, CNS Glasgow Coma Scale, and renal creatinine/urine output).

Quick SOFA (qSOFA—incorporating respiratory rate >=22 breaths/min, altered mentation with GCS <15, and systolic blood pressure <=100 mmHg; 1 point each) is a bedside screening tool to identify patients outside the ICU at high risk of deterioration, but is NOT a diagnostic tool for sepsis.

Septic shock represents a subset of sepsis characterized by cellular and metabolic abnormalities, defined clinically by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP >=65 mmHg AND serum lactate >2.0 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, carrying mortality >40%.

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) 1-hour resuscitation bundle mandates five core actions initiated immediately: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer empiric broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials, administer 30 mL/kg of IV balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >=4 mmol/L, and start vasopressors if MAP remains <65 mmHg.

Lactate clearance (targeting a >=10–20% decrease every 2 hours during the first 6–8 hours of resuscitation) serves as an objective surrogate marker of successful cellular reperfusion and resuscitation efficacy.

uncertainties: Diagnostic superiority of early procalcitonin-guided antibiotic de-escalation protocols versus standardized clinical reassessment.
Personalized fluid resuscitation endpoints utilizing passive leg raise stroke volume variation versus fixed 30 mL/kg volume administration.
mcq_angles: qSOFA components and utility: RR >=22, altered mentation, SBP <=100; validated as a prognostic risk-stratification tool, not a diagnostic criterion for sepsis.
Septic shock diagnostic criteria: concurrent requirement for vasopressor therapy to achieve MAP >=65 mmHg AND elevated serum lactate >2.0 mmol/L despite fluid repletion.
Resuscitation fluid volume: standard recommended crystalloid bolus is 30 mL/kg administered within the first 3 hours of presentation.

page.mentor_intro: Acute native joint septic arthritis is an orthopedic emergency caused by bacterial colonization of the synovial space, predominantly via hematogenous seeding. Prompt diagnostic arthrocentesis and urgent joint decompression are imperative to prevent irreversible chondral degradation and joint destruction.

teaching_points.claim: Acute monoarthritis with joint warmth, swelling, erythema, and severe restriction of both active and passive range of motion must be considered septic arthritis until proven otherwise; the knee is the most commonly affected joint (>50% of cases), followed by the hip, shoulder, and ankle.

Staphylococcus aureus (including Methicillin-resistant S. aureus [MRSA]) is the single most common causative organism overall; Streptococcus pneumoniae and Group A Streptococcus are common in older adults, while Neisseria gonorrhoeae classically affects young, sexually active adults (disseminated gonococcal infection with tenosynovitis and vesiculopustular skin lesions).

Emergency synovial fluid aspiration (arthrocentesis) is mandatory prior to antibiotic administration: synovial fluid analysis typically reveals cloudy or purulent fluid, white blood cell count >50,000/uL with >90% polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs), very low synovial glucose (<50% of blood glucose), and markedly elevated lactate.

Urgent joint decompression via arthroscopic lavage or open arthrotomy is the definitive standard of care for native joints to clear bacterial toxins, inflammatory cytokines, and purulence; needle aspiration alone is acceptable only for easily accessible joints (e.g., knee) in patients responding rapidly to medical therapy.

Empirical intravenous antimicrobial therapy must cover Staphylococcus and Streptococcus (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h or flucloxacillin/cefazolin for MSSA, plus a third-generation cephalosporin like ceftriaxone if gram-negative rods or gonococcal infection is suspected), tailored to culture results and continued for 3 to 4 weeks.

uncertainties: Duration of intravenous versus early oral step-down antibiotic therapy in uncomplicated native joint septic arthritis following complete arthroscopic washout.
Diagnostic accuracy and threshold of synovial fluid alpha-defensin and leukocyte esterase testing in distinguishing culture-negative septic arthritis from severe crystalline arthritis.
mcq_angles: Synovial fluid analysis threshold: WBC count >50,000/uL with >90% neutrophils strongly supports septic arthritis; however, crystal arthropathies (gout/pseudogout) can also exceed this threshold.
Disseminated gonococcal infection triad: migratory polyarthralgias, tenosynovitis, and painless pustular/vesicular skin lesions, often with sterile synovial cultures.
Mandatory surgical principle: complete joint decompression via arthroscopic washout or open arthrotomy must not be delayed to prevent chondral enzymatic necrosis.
case_hooks: A 64-year-old diabetic man presenting with acute right knee pain, inability to bear weight, temperature 38.8 C, and an effusion yielding synovial WBC of 85,000/uL with 95% neutrophils.
A 24-year-old woman presenting with wrist tenosynovitis, fever, scattered painless pustules on her extremities, and acute monoarthritis of the left ankle.

page.mentor_intro: A systematic, protocolized approach to acute monoarthritis ensures prompt diagnosis of septic arthritis before irreversible cartilage damage occurs. Timely synovial fluid analysis, early empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage, and surgical source control form the foundation of management.

teaching_points.claim: Arthrocentesis must be performed urgently before initiating antimicrobial therapy unless systemic septic shock mandates immediate antibiotic administration; synovial fluid must be sent for cell count with differential, Gram stain, polarized microscopy for crystals, bacterial culture, and antimicrobial sensitivities.

Synovial fluid Gram stain provides immediate diagnostic utility but has only moderate sensitivity (approx. 50–60% for Staphylococcal infection, <25% for gonococcal infection, and 40% for gram-negative bacilli); a negative Gram stain NEVER excludes septic arthritis.

Presence of calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD) or monosodium urate (MSU) crystals on polarizing light microscopy does NOT rule out concurrent septic arthritis, as crystal-induced flares and bacterial infection coexist in up to 5% of cases.

Empirical antimicrobial selection is guided by age, host risk factors, and Gram stain: vancomycin covers MRSA; add ceftriaxone (or cefepime/piperacillin-tazobactam in elderly, immunocompromised, or IV drug users) to cover gram-negative bacilli and Pseudomonas.

Surgical drainage options include repeated closed needle aspiration (only for uncomplicated knee infections with thin synovial fluid that clears easily), arthroscopic irrigation and debridement (preferred for knees and shoulders), and open arthrotomy (mandatory for hips, small joints, loculated effusions, or failed arthroscopic clearance).

uncertainties: Clinical utility of point-of-care synovial fluid calprotectin or lactate strips in ruling out septic arthritis in emergency department settings.
Comparative re-operation rates between initial arthroscopic debridement versus primary open arthrotomy in native shoulder septic arthritis.
mcq_angles: Coexistence of crystals and infection: identification of gout or pseudogout crystals does not rule out septic arthritis; synovial culture remains mandatory.
Limitations of Gram stain: false-negative rate is 40–50%; empiric antibiotics should never be withheld solely because of a negative Gram stain if clinical suspicion is high.

Hip septic arthritis drainage rule: septic arthritis of the native hip represents an absolute indication for emergency surgical arthrotomy/arthroscopy due to high intracapsular pressure risking femoral head avascular necrosis.
case_hooks: A 70-year-old man with known gout presenting with acute monoarthritis of the right knee whose synovial fluid shows intracellular needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals and a WBC count of 95,000/uL.
A 4-year-old child who refuses to bear weight on the left leg, holding the left hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated, with fever and elevated ESR/CRP (Kocher criteria).
