page.mentor_intro: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) occurs when normal colonic bacteria colonize the small intestine in abnormal quantities, resulting in malabsorption, chronic diarrhea, bloating, and abdominal pain. Identifying underlying anatomical or motility risk factors and targeted antibiotic decontamination form the diagnostic and treatment core.

teaching_points.claim: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is defined by excessive bacterial density in the small bowel (>10^3 colony-forming units [CFU]/mL on jejunal aspirate culture); it results from failure of normal protective clearance mechanisms: gastric acid barrier, migrating motor complex (MMC) phase III motility, ileocecal valve competence, and mucosal immunoglobulins.

Common predisposing etiologies include structural abnormalities (surgical blind loops, strictures, bariatric Roux-en-Y anatomy, diverticula) and systemic motility disorders (diabetic autonomic enteropathy, systemic sclerosis, chronic opiate use, Parkinson disease).

Non-invasive diagnostic testing utilizes standardized carbohydrate breath testing (glucose or lactulose breath tests); an increase in breath hydrogen of >=20 ppm within 90 minutes confirms hydrogen-predominant SIBO; an elevation in breath methane of >=10 ppm at any point confirms Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth (IMO, predominantly Methanobrevibacter smithii), which is characteristically associated with constipation.

Rifaximin (550 mg orally three times daily for 14 days) is the evidence-based first-line antibiotic of choice for hydrogen-predominant SIBO; it is a minimally absorbed, gut-selective rifamycin that achieves high luminal antimicrobial concentrations with negligible systemic side effects or resistance.

For methane-predominant overgrowth (IMO with constipation), dual combination therapy with rifaximin (550 mg TID) plus oral neomycin (500 mg BID) or metronidazole (250 mg TID) for 14 days achieves significantly higher clinical and microbiological eradication than rifaximin monotherapy.

uncertainties: Efficacy and long-term safety of prokinetic agents (low-dose erythromycin, prucalopride) in preventing recurrent SIBO following antibiotic eradication.
Clinical diagnostic agreement between quantitative small bowel aspirate culture and lactulose versus glucose hydrogen breath tests.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic breath test criteria: hydrogen rise >=20 ppm within 90 minutes indicates hydrogen SIBO; methane level >=10 ppm indicates Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth (IMO).
Clinical correlation of gas types: hydrogen-predominant SIBO is associated with watery diarrhea and malabsorption; methane-predominant overgrowth (IMO) is strongly linked to chronic constipation.
Antibiotic of choice: oral rifaximin (550 mg TID for 14 days) provides non-absorbable targeted luminal decontamination.

page.mentor_intro: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is an exceptionally aggressive, high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma strongly linked to tobacco exposure, characterized by rapid doubling time and early widespread metastatic dissemination. Systemic chemoimmunotherapy has modernized frontline management in extensive-stage disease.

teaching_points.claim: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) represents approximately 15% of all lung cancers, characterized pathologically by small, round-to-oval cells with scant cytoplasm, ill-defined cell borders, granular nuclear chromatin ('salt-and-pepper'), absent nucleoli, frequent crushing artifact, and a Ki-67 proliferation index approaching 100%.

Staging follows the Veterans Administration Lung Group (VALG) classification: Limited-Stage (LS-SCLC, confined to one hemithorax and regional lymph nodes that can be encompassed within a tolerable radiation port; ~30% of patients) and Extensive-Stage (ES-SCLC, disease beyond limited-stage boundaries, including distant metastases, malignant pleural effusion, or bilateral contralateral nodes; ~70%).

For limited-stage SCLC, concurrent chemoradiotherapy (platinum agent [cisplatin preferred] plus etoposide combined with early, concurrent thoracic radiation therapy 45 Gy in 30 twice-daily fractions) is curative-intent standard of care, achieving median survival of 25 to 30 months.

For extensive-stage SCLC, frontline chemoimmunotherapy—platinum and etoposide combined with an immune checkpoint inhibitor (atezolizumab [IMpower133 trial] or durvalumab [CASPIAN trial])—significantly improves progression-free and overall survival compared with platinum-etoposide chemotherapy alone.

Prophylactic Cranial Irradiation (PCI) reduces the incidence of symptomatic brain metastases and improves survival in LS-SCLC patients achieving a complete or good partial response to chemoradiotherapy; in ES-SCLC, routine brain MRI surveillance every 3 months is increasingly preferred over PCI to avoid neurocognitive decline.

uncertainties: Role of consolidation thoracic radiotherapy in extensive-stage SCLC patients demonstrating good distant response to chemoimmunotherapy.
Biomarkers (such as SCLC molecular subtypes SCLC-A, SCLC-N, SCLC-P, and SCLC-I) in predicting individualized immunotherapy benefit.
mcq_angles: Standard frontline regimen for extensive-stage SCLC: platinum (carboplatin or cisplatin) + etoposide + anti-PD-L1 antibody (atezolizumab or durvalumab).
Chemoradiotherapy timing in limited-stage disease: thoracic radiation should be initiated early, concurrently with cycle 1 or 2 of platinum-etoposide.
Prophylactic Cranial Irradiation (PCI) role: indicated in limited-stage SCLC responders to prevent central nervous system recurrence; balanced against neurocognitive toxicity.

page.mentor_intro: Small fiber neuropathy (SFN) selectively affects unmyelinated C-fibers and thinly myelinated A-delta nerve fibers responsible for thermal sensation, nociception, and autonomic function. Because conventional nerve conduction studies are normal, diagnosis relies on skin biopsy quantification of intraepidermal nerve fiber density and specialized autonomic testing.

teaching_points.claim: Small fiber neuropathy presents clinically with burning neuropathic pain, allodynia, hyperalgesia, paresthesias, and dysautonomia (orthostatic intolerance, gastroparesis, secretomotor changes, bowel/bladder dysfunction); large fiber modalities (vibration sense, proprioception, deep tendon reflexes, and muscle strength) are completely preserved.

Routine electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies (NCS) assess only large myelinated A-alpha and A-beta sensory and motor fibers, and are therefore entirely normal in isolated small fiber neuropathy, frequently leading to misdiagnosis.

Punch skin biopsy (typically 3-mm punch taken 10 cm above the lateral malleolus) with immunohistochemical staining for Protein Gene Product 9.5 (PGP 9.5) is the diagnostic gold standard, objectively demonstrating reduced Intraepidermal Nerve Fiber Density (IENFD) below the 5th percentile of age- and sex-adjusted normative values.

Autonomic function testing provides objective confirmation of small fiber involvement: Quantitative Sudomotor Axon Reflex Testing (QSART), thermoregulatory sweat testing (TST), and heart rate variability with deep breathing assess autonomic post-ganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic small fiber function.

Common identifiable secondary etiologies include impaired glucose tolerance/type 2 diabetes (most common), systemic autoimmune conditions (Sjogren syndrome, sarcoidosis, lupus), monoclonal gammopathies, celiac disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A deficiency), and amyloidosis.

uncertainties: Role of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy in autoimmune-mediated or immune-complex small fiber neuropathy.
Diagnostic accuracy of corneal confocal microscopy (measuring corneal sub-basal nerve plexus density) as a non-invasive surrogate for skin biopsy.
mcq_angles: Gold-standard diagnostic test for SFN: skin biopsy with PGP 9.5 quantification showing reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD).
Why nerve conduction studies are normal in SFN: NCS measures only large myelinated A-beta fibers; unmyelinated C and thinly myelinated A-delta fibers cannot be evaluated by routine NCS.
Underlying metabolic cause: impaired glucose tolerance and early prediabetes are the most common identifiable triggers of painful small fiber neuropathy.
case_hooks: A 52-year-old woman with normal fasting glucose but impaired glucose tolerance on OGTT presenting with 12 months of severe burning feet pain and allodynia with normal EMG/NCS.
A 40-year-old man with Sjogren syndrome presenting with orthostatic dizziness, dry skin, and distal paresthesias whose distal leg skin biopsy confirms reduced IENFD at 1.8 fibers/mm.

page.mentor_intro: Tobacco use disorder is a chronic, relapsing condition driven by physical nicotine addiction and behavioral conditioning. Combining first-line evidence-based pharmacotherapy—specifically varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy (NRT)—with behavioral counseling triples long-term smoking cessation rates.

teaching_points.claim: Combining evidence-based pharmacotherapy with structured behavioral counseling (cognitive behavioral strategies, motivational interviewing) is significantly more effective than either modality alone, achieving long-term quit rates 2 to 3 times higher than unassisted quit attempts.

First-line pharmacological options comprise: varenicline (nicotine acetylcholine receptor partial agonist), combination nicotine replacement therapy (NRT: long-acting transdermal patch plus a rapid-acting oral formulation such as gum, lozenge, inhalator, or spray), and bupropion sustained-release (atypical antidepressant and dopamine/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor).

In high-quality network meta-analyses and randomized trials (e.g., EAGLES trial), varenicline and combination NRT demonstrate equivalent superior efficacy, both achieving significantly higher 6-month abstinence rates (approx. 25–30%) compared with bupropion monotherapy (15–20%) or single-agent NRT.

Varenicline binds with high affinity to alpha-4-beta-2 neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors as a partial agonist: stimulating moderate dopamine release in the mesolimbic reward system to alleviate nicotine craving and withdrawal symptoms, while competitively blocking nicotine from binding to blunt the rewarding effects of smoking.

The landmark EAGLES randomized trial (over 8,000 smokers with and without psychiatric disorders) firmly refuted historical neuropsychiatric warnings, demonstrating that varenicline and bupropion do NOT increase the incidence of serious neuropsychiatric adverse events (depression, suicidal ideation) compared with placebo or NRT.

Contraindications and safety pearls: bupropion is strictly contraindicated in patients with a history of seizure disorder, eating disorders (anorexia/bulimia), or abrupt alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal due to a lowered seizure threshold; varenicline common side effects include nausea (minimized by taking with food and water) and vivid dreams.

uncertainties: Long-term cardiovascular and pulmonary safety profiles of electronic nicotine delivery systems (e-cigarettes/vaping) utilized as smoking cessation tools.
Optimal treatment duration of maintenance varenicline (extended 24 weeks vs standard 12 weeks) in heavy relapsing smokers.
mcq_angles: EAGLES trial landmark finding: varenicline does not increase serious neuropsychiatric adverse events or suicidality in smokers with or without psychiatric history.
Most effective pharmacotherapy options: varenicline monotherapy and combination NRT (patch + rapid-acting oral NRT) are equally superior to single-agent NRT or bupropion.
Bupropion contraindication: seizure disorder, active eating disorders, and abrupt withdrawal from alcohol or sedatives due to heightened seizure risk.
case_hooks: A 45-year-old heavy smoker (20 cigarettes/day for 25 years) with stable depression on sertraline seeking the most effective pharmacotherapy to quit smoking permanently.
A 38-year-old man with a history of idiopathic generalized epilepsy inquiring whether bupropion is safe to use for tobacco cessation.

page.mentor_intro: Asplenic and hyposplenic patients are at lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection from encapsulated bacteria. Prevention rests on vaccination, antibiotic prophylaxis, a standby antibiotic supply and patient education.

teaching_points.claim: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is most often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (about half or more), then Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b.

Vaccines (pneumococcal conjugate and polysaccharide, Hib, MenACWY, MenB, and annual influenza) should be given at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy, or about 2 weeks afterwards after emergency splenectomy.
Patients keep standby antibiotics to take at the first sign of fever, shivering or chills while seeking urgent medical help, and carry an alert card.
Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is advised for high-risk groups, commonly lifelong or for at least 2 years after splenectomy and until age 16, per local policy.
Travel advice should include malaria prevention and avoiding animal bites (Capnocytophaga).

teaching_points.claim: Clinical practice guideline consensus establishes evidence-directed diagnostic criteria and risk-stratified therapy for stemi: electrocardiographic mimics and reperfusion decision: Evidence-Based Clinical Practice and Multi-Society Consensus on STEMI: electrocardiographic mimics and reperfusion decision.

Important electrocardiographic mimics of STEMI include acute pericarditis (diffuse concave ST elevation with PR segment depression), benign early repolarization, left ventricular hypertrophy (voltage criteria with strain pattern), and Brugada syndrome.

In patients with left bundle branch block (LBBB) or ventricular paced rhythm, modified Sgarbossa criteria identify acute coronary occlusion: concordant ST elevation >=1 mm, concordant ST depression >=1 mm in V1-V3, or excessively discordant ST elevation/S-wave ratio <= -0.25.

Emergent coronary angiography is indicated in patients with resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and ST elevation on ECG, or in patients with hemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock, or persistent ischemic chest pain despite equivocal ECG findings.

page.mentor_intro: Prompt reperfusion is the cornerstone of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) management. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the gold standard when achievable within guideline-mandated timeframes, while fibrinolytic therapy serves as an essential alternative when transfer delays preclude timely catheterization.

teaching_points.claim: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the preferred reperfusion strategy when it can be performed within 120 minutes of STEMI diagnosis; in PCI-capable centers, the target door-to-balloon time is under 90 minutes (or under 60 minutes for direct presentation).

When anticipated delay from STEMI diagnosis to PCI exceeds 120 minutes, emergency intravenous fibrinolysis (tenecteplase weight-adjusted bolus) should be administered within 10 minutes of diagnosis, followed by immediate transfer to a PCI center for routine pharmacoinvasive angiography within 2 to 24 hours.

Dual antiplatelet therapy comprising aspirin (150-300 mg loading dose) plus a potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 180 mg or prasugrel 60 mg) is superior to clopidogrel in reducing ischemic events and stent thrombosis without excess overall mortality.
Radial artery access is strongly recommended over femoral access (Class I, Level A) to reduce major vascular bleeding complications, access-site hematomas, and 30-day all-cause mortality.

uncertainties: Timing of non-culprit lesion revascularization: immediate multivessel PCI during the index procedure versus staged inpatient intervention.
Optimal duration of dual antiplatelet therapy in patients at high bleeding risk receiving contemporary drug-eluting stents.
mcq_angles: Reperfusion timeframe rules: transfer for primary PCI if FMC-to-device is <120 minutes; otherwise immediate fibrinolysis within 10 minutes.
Contraindications to fibrinolysis: prior intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke within 6 months, active internal bleeding, known intracranial neoplasm.
Vascular access selection: radial artery access significantly reduces mortality and major bleeding compared to femoral access in STEMI.

page.mentor_intro: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage is a neurosurgical emergency. After securing the aneurysm, nimodipine reduces poor outcome, delayed cerebral ischaemia is watched for between days 4 and 14, and triple-H therapy is no longer used.

teaching_points.claim: Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days improves outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage; its benefit is not due to preventing angiographic vasospasm.
Delayed cerebral ischaemia typically occurs between days 4 and 14 and is monitored by neurological examination with transcranial Doppler or CT angiography/perfusion.
Treatment of delayed ischaemia aims for euvolaemia and induced hypertension if needed; routine hypervolaemia and haemodilution (triple-H therapy) are no longer recommended.
The aneurysm is secured early, by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping; ISAT favoured coiling for suitable aneurysms.

page.mentor_intro: Suspected melanoma needs urgent specialist assessment and complete excision biopsy. Dermoscopy improves accuracy, and Breslow thickness determines wide excision margins and sentinel node biopsy.

teaching_points.claim: Pigmented lesions with asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variegation, diameter of 6 mm or more or evolution (ABCDE), or an 'ugly duckling' lesion, warrant urgent suspected-cancer referral.
Diagnosis is by complete excision biopsy with a narrow (about 2 mm) margin; incisional or shave biopsy is avoided where possible because accurate Breslow thickness drives management.
Dermoscopy raises diagnostic accuracy; melanoma features include an atypical network, irregular globules, blue-white veil and regression structures.
Wide local excision margins depend on Breslow thickness: 1 cm for in situ to 1 mm tumours, and 1 to 2 cm for 1 to 2 mm, with 2 cm (2 to 3 cm in UK guidance) for tumours thicker than 2 mm.
Sentinel lymph node biopsy is offered for tumours of about 0.8 mm or thicker, or thinner with ulceration.

page.mentor_intro: Symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure) is treated with atropine, then second-line drugs or pacing. Infranodal block often fails to respond to atropine.

teaching_points.claim: For unstable bradycardia, give atropine 500 mcg to 1 mg IV every 3 to 5 minutes up to 3 mg; it is often ineffective in infranodal (Mobitz II or complete) block, in heart transplant recipients and in some drug overdoses.
If atropine fails, options are transcutaneous pacing, adrenaline 2 to 10 mcg/min, or dopamine 5 to 20 mcg/kg/min while arranging transvenous pacing.
Transcutaneous pacing is painful and needs analgesia and sedation; it is a bridge.
Mobitz II, complete heart block with a wide QRS, or ventricular pauses of 3 seconds or more call for urgent transvenous pacing and planning for a permanent pacemaker.

page.mentor_intro: Evaluation of syncope requires distinguishing benign reflex/orthostatic etiologies from life-threatening cardiogenic causes. Permanent pacemaker implantation is indicated for high-grade atrioventricular block, symptomatic sick sinus syndrome, and severe cardioinhibitory reflex syncope meeting strict diagnostic criteria.

teaching_points.claim: Diagnostic workup of syncope prioritizes distinguishing cardiac (arrhythmic or structural) causes from vasovagal and orthostatic syncope; persistent unexplained syncope in patients with underlying structural heart disease or abnormal baseline ECG carries high risk of sudden cardiac death.

Class I indications for permanent cardiac pacing in acquired atrioventricular (AV) block include complete third-degree AV block, advanced/high-grade second-degree AV block, and Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block, regardless of symptoms.

In sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction), pacing is indicated only when syncope or presyncope is directly documented to correlate with symptomatic sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, or sinoatrial exit block.

For recurrent cardioinhibitory reflex syncope in patients aged >=40 years, dual-chamber pacemaker implantation is indicated when documentation of asystolic pauses >=3 seconds (with syncope) or >=6 seconds (asymptomatic) is confirmed during tilt-table testing or implantable loop recorder (ILR) monitoring.

uncertainties: Efficacy of closed-loop stimulation (CLS) pacing versus conventional dual-chamber DDD pacing in suppressing vasovagal syncope recurrence.

mcq_angles: ECG red flags in syncope: bifascicular block, Mobitz II second-degree AV block, prolonged QT interval, Brugada pattern, or pre-excitation (WPW).
Pacing threshold in carotid sinus hypersensitivity: reproduction of syncope with asystole >3 seconds during carotid sinus massage confirms cardioinhibitory subtype.
Mobitz I vs Mobitz II pacing indications: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) usually does not require pacing unless symptomatic; Mobitz II always warrants permanent pacing.

page.mentor_intro: Syncope evaluation starts with history, examination, orthostatic blood pressure and ECG to separate reflex, orthostatic and cardiac causes. Implantable loop recorders have the best yield for recurrent unexplained syncope.

teaching_points.claim: Features suggesting cardiac syncope include sudden onset without prodrome, onset during exertion or supine, abnormal ECG and structural heart disease; reflex syncope has triggers and prodrome.
Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed by a sustained systolic fall of 20 mmHg or diastolic 10 mmHg (or systolic below 90) within 3 minutes of standing.
Implantable loop recorders have a higher diagnostic yield than Holter monitoring or tilt testing for recurrent unexplained syncope of suspected arrhythmic origin.
Carotid sinus massage is considered in patients over 40 with unexplained syncope; a ventricular pause over 3 seconds or systolic fall of 50 mmHg or more indicates carotid sinus syndrome.
Tilt-table testing helps diagnose reflex syncope in selected cases.

page.mentor_intro: Syphilis is staged clinically, confirmed with treponemal and non-treponemal serology, and treated with benzathine penicillin G for early and late latent disease, and intravenous benzylpenicillin for neurosyphilis.

teaching_points.claim: Primary syphilis presents with a painless indurated chancre; secondary with a non-itchy rash including palms and soles, condylomata lata and lymphadenopathy.
Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent) is treated with a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM.
Late latent and tertiary syphilis (gummatous, cardiovascular) are treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 weeks.

Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and otosyphilis are treated with IV benzylpenicillin 18 to 24 million units daily for 10 to 14 days; lumbar puncture is performed when neurological, ocular or otic features are present.
Diagnosis uses a treponemal test (EIA/TPPA) with a non-treponemal titre (RPR/VDRL); treatment response is a fourfold titre fall, and the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may follow the first dose.

teaching_points.claim: Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: Efficacy of different pharmacological therapies for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.

Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc, formerly CREST syndrome) features skin thickening restricted to hands, face, and distal limbs, strongly correlates with anti-centromere antibodies (ACA), and has high late risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).

Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) features proximal limb and truncal skin involvement, anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) or anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies, and high early risk of progressive interstitial lung disease and scleroderma renal crisis.

Systemic sclerosis patients require annual screening for pulmonary hypertension using transthoracic echocardiography, DLCO, and the DETECT algorithm, confirming elevated pulmonary pressures with right heart catheterization.

Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis primarily affecting the aorta and its major branches in young females, presenting with limb claudication, pulse deficits, and vascular bruits; high-dose systemic corticosteroids combined with early steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (methotrexate, tocilizumab, or TNF inhibitors like infliximab) induce remission and prevent irreversible vascular stenosis or aneurysm formation.

Revascularization (endovascular angioplasty, stenting, or bypass surgery) should be strictly avoided during active acute vascular inflammation and performed only once stable medical remission is achieved to prevent restenosis and graft thrombosis.

teaching_points.claim: Contemporary evidence synthesis highlights core pathophysiology, clinical staging, and multidisciplinary management: Advances in tuberculosis treatment: novel regimens, new drug pipelines, host-directed therapies, and updated management guidelines.

Standard first-line therapy for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis comprises a 2-month intensive phase with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE), followed by a 4-month continuation phase with rifampicin and isoniazid (RI).

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) requires withholding hepatotoxic drugs (pyrazinamide > isoniazid > rifampicin) if serum transaminases exceed 5 times the upper limit of normal (or 3 times ULN with symptoms of jaundice, nausea, or abdominal pain).

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6, 25-50 mg daily) is routinely co-administered with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy, especially in patients with diabetes, alcohol dependence, renal failure, malnutrition, or pregnancy.

page.mentor_intro: Tetanus is prevented by immunisation and wound management. Established tetanus needs intensive care, human tetanus immunoglobulin, wound debridement, metronidazole and control of spasms and autonomic instability.

teaching_points.claim: Wounds are classed as clean/minor or tetanus-prone (puncture, soil or faecal contamination, devitalised tissue, burns); vaccine boosters are given if the primary course is incomplete or the last dose was too long ago for the wound class.
Tetanus immunoglobulin (about 250 IU IM, 500 IU for heavy contamination or after 24 hours) is given for tetanus-prone wounds in people with unknown or incomplete immunisation.
Established tetanus presents with trismus, risus sardonicus, painful spasms and autonomic instability.

Management is ICU care, wound debridement, human tetanus immunoglobulin (a large dose, for example 3,000 to 6,000 IU IM), metronidazole in preference to penicillin, benzodiazepines and magnesium for spasm, and ventilation when needed.

Contemporary evidence synthesis highlights core pathophysiology, clinical staging, and multidisciplinary management: Goodpasture syndrome and anti-glomerular basement membrane disease.

Thin basement membrane nephropathy (benign familial hematuria) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by heterozygous mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4, characterized by persistent microscopic hematuria with normal kidney function and minimal proteinuria; renal biopsy on electron microscopy shows uniform, diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane (<250 nm in adults) without the lamellation or podocyte foot-process effacement characteristic of Alport syndrome.

Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are indicated in patients with thin basement membrane nephropathy who develop overt proteinuria (>0.5-1.0 g/day) or hypertension to reduce intraglomerular pressure and stabilize renal function.

page.mentor_intro: Third, fourth, and sixth cranial nerve palsies: pupil-sparing oculomotor palsy is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

teaching_points.claim: Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: Botulinum Toxin Injection for the Treatment of Third, Fourth, and Sixth Nerve Palsy: A Meta-Analysis.

An acute isolated third cranial nerve (oculomotor) palsy with pupillary involvement (dilated, unreactive pupil) or partial pupillary involvement represents a neurological emergency mandating immediate CT angiography or catheter angiography to exclude an intracranial aneurysm (most commonly of the posterior communicating artery, PCoA); complete pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in patients with cardiovascular risk factors is typically caused by microvascular ischemia, which resolves spontaneously over 8-12 weeks.

Fourth cranial nerve (trochlear) palsy presents with vertical diplopia worsening on downgaze and head tilt toward the affected side, with patients adopting a compensatory head tilt away from the affected side (Bielschowsky head tilt test).

Sixth cranial nerve (abducens) palsy causes horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze towards the affected eye; in elderly patients, isolated abducens palsy is frequently microvascular, but in younger patients, elevated intracranial pressure or MS must be excluded.

page.mentor_intro: Long-term surveillance for differentiated thyroid carcinoma (papillary and follicular) utilizes high-resolution cervical ultrasonography and serial serum thyroglobulin measurements. Risk-stratified follow-up allows tailoring of TSH suppression therapy and avoids unnecessary invasive imaging in patients achieving an excellent response to treatment.

teaching_points.claim: Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) measured alongside anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb) is the primary sensitive tumor marker for recurrent differentiated thyroid carcinoma following total thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation; any presence of TgAb invalidates automated immunometric Tg assays and mandates radioimmunoassay or LC-MS/MS measurement.

High-resolution neck ultrasonography performed at 6 to 12 months post-ablation and periodically thereafter evaluates the central and lateral cervical nodal basins; suspicious features include microcalcifications, round shape, cystic necrosis, hyperechoic punctate foci, and loss of the fatty hilum.

According to the American Thyroid Association (ATA) dynamic risk stratification, patients are reclassified into excellent response, biochemically incomplete response, structurally incomplete response, or indeterminate response based on follow-up imaging and stimulated/unstimulated Tg levels.

In patients achieving an 'excellent response' (undetectable unstimulated Tg <0.2 ng/mL or stimulated Tg <1 ng/mL with negative imaging), TSH targets are relaxed to the normal reference range (0.5-2.0 mIU/L), minimizing iatrogenic risks of osteoporosis and atrial fibrillation.

uncertainties: Optimal interval for routine ultrasound surveillance in low-risk patients who maintain undetectable thyroglobulin beyond 5 years.
Clinical threshold for empiric radioiodine therapy versus surveillance in patients with biochemically incomplete response without structural localization.
mcq_angles: Laboratory pitfall with thyroglobulin: anti-Tg antibodies falsely lower immunometric Tg measurements; serial monitoring must always include concurrent TgAb titers.
Lymph node biopsy threshold: suspicious cervical lymph nodes should undergo ultrasound-guided FNA with needle washout for Tg measurement when measuring >=8-10 mm in smallest diameter.
TSH suppression targets: maintain TSH <0.1 mIU/L for high-risk persistent disease, 0.1-0.5 mIU/L for intermediate risk, and 0.5-2.0 mIU/L for low-risk complete responders.
case_hooks: A 46-year-old woman 1 year post-total thyroidectomy and 131-I ablation whose serum Tg is undetectable (<0.1 ng/mL) but anti-Tg antibody rises from 15 to 140 IU/mL.
A 55-year-old man with treated papillary thyroid cancer whose routine surveillance ultrasound detects a 12-mm round, hypoechoic lymph node in level IV with microcalcifications.

teaching_points.claim: Clinical practice guideline consensus establishes evidence-directed diagnostic criteria and risk-stratified therapy for thyroiditis: hashimotos, de quervains, postpartum - phases, tsh trajectory, management: Evidence-Based Clinical Practice and Multi-Society Consensus on Thyroiditis: Hashimotos, de Quervains, postpartum - phases, TSH trajectory, management.

Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) and postpartum thyroiditis classically follow a triphasic clinical and biochemical trajectory: an initial thyrotoxic phase (caused by follicular disruption and release of preformed hormone, characterized by low radioiodine/technetium uptake) lasting 2-8 weeks, followed by a transient hypothyroid phase, and eventual euthyroid recovery in >90% of cases; thyrotoxic symptoms are treated with beta-blockers rather than antithyroid drugs (which are ineffective).

Hashimoto thyroiditis is characterized by elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies leading to chronic autoimmune destruction and permanent hypothyroidism requiring lifelong levothyroxine.

Subacute de Quervain thyroiditis typically presents with severe anterior neck pain radiating to the jaw, markedly elevated ESR/CRP, and rapid relief following nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or oral corticosteroids.

page.mentor_intro: Evaluation of thyroid nodules is guided by ultrasound pattern risk stratification according to the American Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines or ACR TI-RADS. Determining when to perform fine-needle aspiration (FNA) balances identifying clinically significant thyroid carcinomas against avoiding overdiagnosis of indolent microcarcinomas.

teaching_points.claim: Ultrasound features associated with high suspicion of malignancy (ATA high risk: >70-90% cancer risk) include solid hypoechoic composition, irregular or microlobulated margins, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide shape, and rim calcifications with small extrusive soft-tissue components.

Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) is recommended for high-suspicion nodules >=1.0 cm, intermediate-suspicion nodules >=1.0 cm, low-suspicion nodules >=1.5 cm, and very low-suspicion nodules >=2.0 cm; purely cystic nodules carry <1% malignancy risk and do not require diagnostic biopsy.

Initial biochemical workup requires checking serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH); a suppressed TSH warrants radionuclide thyroid scintigraphy (I-123 or Tc-99m) to detect hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodules, which are rarely malignant and do not require FNA.

Cytological results are classified according to the Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology (Categories I to VI), where Category III (AUS/FLUS) and Category IV (Follicular Neoplasm) represent indeterminate lesions suitable for molecular diagnostic testing (e.g., Afirma, ThyroSeq) to avoid unnecessary diagnostic hemithyroidectomy.

uncertainties: Cost-effectiveness and long-term diagnostic utility of reflex molecular testing in Bethesda III nodules with low-risk sonographic appearance.
Active surveillance protocols versus immediate surgery for biopsy-proven low-risk micropapillary thyroid carcinomas (<1 cm).
mcq_angles: First step in thyroid nodule workup: serum TSH measurement; if low, perform scintigraphy before considering FNA.
Most specific ultrasound predictor of papillary thyroid cancer: punctate microcalcifications (psammoma bodies) and taller-than-wide geometry.
Size threshold rule: nodules <1.0 cm without extrathyroidal extension, regional lymphadenopathy, or high-risk clinical features do not undergo routine FNA regardless of sonographic appearance.

teaching_points.claim: Clinical practice guideline consensus establishes evidence-directed diagnostic criteria and risk-stratified therapy for thyroid storm: burch-wartofsky score, propylthiouracil, beta-blockade, supportive care: Evidence-Based Clinical Practice and Multi-Society Consensus on Thyroid storm: Burch-Wartofsky score, propylthiouracil, beta-blockade, supportive care.

The Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS score >=45 highly suggestive) quantifies end-organ dysfunction (thermoregulatory, CNS agitation/coma, cardiovascular tachyarrhythmias, heart failure, and GI-hepatic dysfunction) to establish clinical diagnosis without awaiting lab confirmation.

Multimodal medical therapy follows a strict sequence: (1) high-dose antithyroid drug (propylthiouracil 200 mg every 4 hours preferred over methimazole due to inhibition of peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion); (2) inorganic iodine (Lugols solution or SSKI) administered at least 1 hour AFTER antithyroid drugs to block thyroid hormone release without providing substrate; (3) beta-blockers (propranolol); and (4) intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg every 8 hours) to prevent adrenal crisis and inhibit peripheral deiodination.

Supportive management includes aggressive active cooling (avoiding aspirin, which displaces thyroid hormone from binding globulins), broad-spectrum treatment of underlying precipitating triggers (sepsis, surgery, DKA), and bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine) to disrupt enterohepatic hormone recirculation.

Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) typically presents with a biphasic clinical course: an initial viremic phase with flu-like symptoms, followed by an asymptomatic interval and a second neurological phase (meningitis, meningoencephalitis, or poliomyelitis-like flaccid paralysis).

TBE diagnosis is established by detecting specific IgM and IgG antibodies in serum and CSF (ELISA); no specific antiviral therapy exists, making supportive care and pre-exposure vaccination with inactivated TBE vaccine the mainstay of management.

In patients with active axial spondyloarthritis who fail or cannot tolerate first-line NSAIDs, TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, certolizumab, golimumab) or IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) are equally recommended as first-line biologics.

IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) are contraindicated in patients with active inflammatory bowel disease (Crohns disease, ulcerative colitis) due to risks of precipitating disease exacerbation, making TNF monoclonal antibodies preferred.

For patients presenting with recurrent anterior uveitis complicating axSpA, monoclonal TNF antibodies (adalimumab, certolizumab, infliximab) are superior to etanercept and IL-17 inhibitors in preventing uveitis flares.

page.mentor_intro: TNF inhibitors treat rheumatoid arthritis that has failed conventional DMARDs. Screening for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B is required before starting, and certain conditions contraindicate use.

teaching_points.claim: TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab) are used in active rheumatoid arthritis despite conventional DMARDs, usually with methotrexate.
Before treatment, screen for latent tuberculosis (IGRA or tuberculin test, with chest radiograph) and hepatitis B and C.
Contraindications include active serious infection, NYHA class III to IV heart failure, and demyelinating disease.
Methotrexate co-therapy lowers anti-drug antibody formation, especially with monoclonal antibodies such as infliximab and adalimumab.
For major elective surgery the drug is usually withheld for one to two dosing intervals and restarted after wound healing, per local policy.

page.mentor_intro: TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS) is an autosomal dominant systemic autoinflammatory disorder caused by mutations in the TNFRSF1A gene. Characterized by prolonged febrile episodes lasting weeks, migratory myalgias with overlying fasciitis, and periorbital edema, TRAPS carries a substantial risk of secondary AA amyloidosis.

teaching_points.claim: TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS) is an autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder caused by mutations in the TNFRSF1A gene (encoding the 55-kDa TNF receptor type 1), leading to protein misfolding, defective receptor clearance, ligand-independent intracellular signaling, and hyperactivation of the IL-1 beta pathway.

Clinical attacks typically persist for 1 to 3 weeks (significantly longer than the 1-3 day attacks in familial Mediterranean fever) and feature prolonged spiking fevers, centrifugal painful migratory erythematous plaques with underlying monocytic fasciitis, periorbital edema, serositis, and severe arthralgias.

Secondary reactive (AA) amyloidosis represents the most severe long-term complication, developing in up to 15-25% of untreated patients with structural pathogenic mutations (e.g., cysteine residue substitutions) and manifesting as progressive proteinuria and renal failure.

Targeted cytokine inhibition with interleukin-1 antagonists (canakinumab, anakinra) is the evidence-based first-line therapy, achieving rapid clinical remission, biochemical normalization of CRP/SAA, and effective prevention of amyloidosis; NSAIDs provide only partial symptomatic relief, and etanercept shows diminishing long-term efficacy.

uncertainties: Clinical penetrance and treatment thresholds for low-penetrance variants (such as R92Q and P46L) presenting with atypical mild autoinflammatory symptoms.
Long-term strategy for on-demand versus continuous maintenance dosing with canakinumab in adult TRAPS.
mcq_angles: Attack duration comparison: TRAPS episodes last 1 to 4 weeks, contrasting with FMF (12-72 hours) and HIDS/MKD (3-7 days).
Characteristic physical signs: migratory erythematous plaques over deep muscular fasciitis and unilateral/bilateral periorbital edema.
Therapeutic drug of choice: IL-1 blockade (canakinumab/anakinra) is superior to TNF inhibitors (etanercept) in maintaining complete disease remission.
case_hooks: A 28-year-old woman presenting with a 14-day history of high fevers, severe thigh pain with overlying warm erythematous rash, periorbital edema, and elevated CRP of 180 mg/L.
A 35-year-old man with childhood-onset periodic fever syndromes who develops nephrotic-range proteinuria and renal biopsy-proven apple-green birefringent deposits on Congo red staining.
